newsitem.title: USA: U.S. ridicules Iraqi spy claim.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ridicules Iraqi spy claim.

text.p: The State Department on Friday dismissed Iraqi claims to have uncovered a CIA spy network as "laughable propaganda" and said anyone who believed them "ought to have their heads examined."
The Central Intelligence Agency declined comment on the report by the Iraqi News Agency, which said members of the group had admitted carrying out spying activities in Iraq.
"Frankly, if anybody believes these reports they ought to have their heads examined," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

"This is a well-noted and tired propaganda ploy," Burns said. "There's always got to be a scapegoat for the problems of a corrupt, authoritarian dictatorship like Saddam's," he said referring to Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
"He looks on the outside and what more convenient target than than the Central Intelligence Agency? This is laughable propaganda," Burns told a news briefing.

The U.S. spokesman invited sympathy for the "poor Iraqis" accused of being spies. "They've probably picked them up off the street, and they didn't like their looks, didn't like their politics, and they shove them in front of TV cameras and they throw them in jail to rot," he said.
Another U.S. official suggested the Iraqi report was aimed at showing Saddam's eldest son Uday was in control after surviving an apparent assassination attempt last week.
"I don't think that this is a new development," the official said.

He said any Iraqis put on display as alleged CIA agents could include some of those detained by Saddam in early September after Iraqi forces drove into a Western-protected Kurdish safe haven in Northern Iraq.
The official added that when the Iraqis capture suspected spies they typically "grill them" for months.

According to Iraqi dissident groups, when the Iraqi forces marched into the Kurdish enclave, they broke up a long-standing CIA-funded covert operation to destabilize Saddam Hussein. More than 100 Iraqis were arrested and executed and others were taken prisoner, according to the dissident groups.
The movement of Iraqi troops into the Kurdish enclave in August in support of one of the Kurdish factions there sparked renewed tension with the United States.
To punish Saddam at the time, the United States launched cruise missiles against Iraqi air defenses and expanded the Western-enforced no-fly zone in Iraq.
